accuracyBoundary: These chapters teach mechanisms and decision logic. Material-grade processing windows, machine limits, mould limits, hot-runner limits and site procedures remain controlling. Numeric examples from manufacturer documents are evidence examples only and are not universal setpoints.

chapters.title: What plastic is made of: polymer structure and cooling
chapters.applicability: General thermoplastic concepts. Exact material behaviour depends on the supplier grade and how it is processed.

sections.title: Start here: plastic is made of long chains
sections.text:
Most plastics used in injection moulding are made from very long molecules called polymer chains. A useful first picture is a bowl of cooked spaghetti: each strand stands for one chain, and many chains sit close together. The comparison helps you imagine long molecules, but it is only a picture. Real chains are far too small to see, move continually, and interact in ways that a bowl of spaghetti cannot show.

The visible pellets fed to a machine are pieces of material; they are not single polymer chains. Each pellet contains many chains and may also contain colourants, fibres, fillers or other ingredients. The chain structure and any added ingredients help explain why two plastics can look similar but respond differently to heat, flow and cooling.

When a thermoplastic is heated, its chains gain mobility and the material can soften and flow. As it cools, chain movement slows and the moulding becomes solid. Some plastics are described as amorphous: their chains do not form the same ordered crystalline regions during cooling. Other plastics are semi-crystalline: parts of their structure can form ordered regions while other areas remain less ordered. “Semi” matters—the whole part is not one perfect crystal.

These labels give you a starting model, not a complete prediction. The exact grade, its formulation and the part’s local flow and cooling history still matter. A thin region and a thick region of one part may not experience the same history. Use the chain picture to ask better questions about the material; do not use it to select machine settings or assume how a finished part will behave.

sections.title: Repeat units and chain size
sections.text:
A polymer chain is a macromolecule: one very large molecule built from a repeating chemical pattern. The repeating pattern is called a repeat unit. The spaghetti picture is useful for length and entanglement; it does not show the chemical groups that give each polymer its identity.

A resin is not normally a box containing identical chains of one exact length. It contains a population of molecules with different chain lengths and, depending on the chemistry, different structures. Scientists describe that population using averages and a molecular-weight distribution. “Molecular weight” in polymer records usually refers to molecular mass expressed with conventional terminology. A single average is a summary of a population, not a photograph of every molecule.

This distinction helps explain why two products from one broad family can still be different materials. Their chain lengths, distribution, branching, comonomers, additives and reinforcement may differ. Each feature can matter in a different way, and the effect depends on the polymer and the application. The family name is therefore an orientation label; the complete commercial grade is still needed to connect a scientific idea to supplier data.

Keep the scale in mind. Pellets are visible pieces containing many polymer molecules. A molecular chain is far smaller than a pellet or a moulded part. A part drawing describes shape and dimensions; it does not reveal the molecules inside it. Polymer science links those scales through measurements, but no single label or measurement describes every aspect of a finished part.

sections.title: Molecular-weight distribution, branching and entanglement
sections.text:
In a polymer melt, long molecules move among and around one another. Many chains become temporarily entangled, much like strands in a dense bowl of noodles. These entanglements are physical constraints on motion, not permanent chemical links between chains. When heat and time allow, chains can rearrange and relax some of the stresses created by flow.

Chain length and branching change that molecular motion. A molecular-weight distribution tells us that a sample contains a range of chain sizes. Branches change the shape and the ways chains can relax. Their effects depend on polymer chemistry and on the kind and amount of branching; “more branches” is not a universal instruction for predicting one property.

A primary study of low-density polyethylene separated material fractions by crystallisability and molecular weight, then measured their rheology. In those LDPE fractions, molecular weight strongly influenced measured behaviour, and long-chain branching affected some measured responses, including extension. That is useful evidence that molecular architecture can matter. It is a result for the tested LDPE and methods, not a transferable rule for every plastic family or every moulding grade.

Rheology is the study of how a material flows and deforms. A polymer melt is viscoelastic: its response combines liquid-like flow with time-dependent elastic behaviour. The balance depends on the material and the test conditions. This is why a polymer cannot be described fully by saying only that it is “thick” or “thin.” A laboratory measurement under one test does not automatically predict every flow path, pressure history or part result in a mould.

Use these ideas to frame questions rather than guess settings. If a family or grade behaves differently from expectation, the useful next step is to confirm the exact grade and compare evidence measured under suitable conditions. Molecular architecture helps explain why the question matters; the supplier’s current grade information and the actual part evidence still control the decision.

sections.title: Glass transition, melting and crystallisation are different events
sections.text:
Three temperature terms are easy to confuse. The glass-transition temperature, often written Tg, describes a change in molecular mobility in amorphous regions. It is not the same as melting. In a semi-crystalline polymer, crystalline regions have their own melting transition, often described by Tm. Crystallisation is the formation of ordered regions as suitable parts of a polymer melt cool. The terms describe different physical events.

A semi-crystalline material is not a solid block made entirely of crystals. It contains ordered crystalline regions and less-ordered amorphous regions. The proportions and arrangement can vary with the grade and the material’s thermal history. An amorphous polymer does not form the same crystalline structure during cooling, but its molecular mobility and response still change with temperature. These labels describe useful parts of the structure; they do not give a complete property card for the grade.

Differential scanning calorimetry, or DSC, measures heat flow while a controlled sample is heated or cooled. Depending on the material and method, DSC can help identify glass transitions, melting and crystallisation events. ISO 11357-1 describes general principles for DSC testing of plastics, including sampling, calibration and reporting. A DSC trace belongs to the sample and test programme that produced it. It is not a direct temperature map of every location in a production moulding.

When reading a transition temperature, keep the method and thermal history beside the number. A reported transition helps explain what happened in a test. It does not by itself prescribe a machine setting or guarantee how a component will perform in service.

sections.title: Cooling rate can change the crystallisation path
sections.text:
Crystallisation is a process that takes time. When a semi-crystalline polymer cools from a melt, molecular segments need opportunities to organise into ordered regions. The cooling path can therefore influence what develops before the material becomes too immobile. The grade, pressure, additives and local conditions also matter, so cooling rate is one influence in a larger material-and-process history.

A primary study used fast-scanning differential scanning calorimetry to examine one semi-crystalline polypropylene. In the tested sample, higher cooling rates were associated with lower measured crystallisation temperatures and lower measured crystallinity. This is a result for that polypropylene and the study’s measurement conditions. It is not a numerical rule for every PP grade, another polymer family or a production part.

A moulded wall does not cool as one perfectly uniform slab. The surface and interior have different heat-transfer paths, while thickness, geometry and local flow history can differ across the part. That is one reason morphology—the arrangement and distribution of structural regions—can vary by position. A later dimensional or performance difference may therefore need a part-level investigation rather than an assumption based on the polymer-family label.

For a beginner, the safe interpretation is simple: cooling history can be part of the material’s structural history, and the effect must be tied to the exact grade and evidence. Do not copy a laboratory cooling rate into a machine recipe. Use the supplier’s current grade guidance and the applicable product and site validation process.

sections.title: Different instruments answer different polymer questions
sections.text:
Polymer scientists choose a measurement for the question they need to answer. Size-exclusion or gel-permeation chromatography can be used to study molecular-weight distributions, subject to the method and calibration used. DSC is used to investigate thermal events such as glass transition, melting and crystallisation. X-ray micro-computed tomography can reveal three-dimensional fibre-orientation patterns in a reinforced specimen. These tools do not all measure the same feature.

A result also has limits. A measured molecular-weight distribution does not tell you the exact orientation of fibres in a moulded rib. A DSC trace does not map the temperature history of every point in a production mould. A micro-CT image describes the sampled material and location; it does not by itself prove that an entire product meets its requirements. The method, sample, grade and conditions belong with the result.

This is why a material review may combine different kinds of evidence: the exact supplier grade and its current technical documents, a measurement selected for the question, and checks on the actual part under the product’s defined conditions. If the evidence does not answer a question, record it as unknown rather than filling the gap with a generic family assumption.

The useful polymer-science habit is to name the thing being measured. Is the question about chain-size distribution, a thermal transition, local fibre orientation, a supplier-reported property or the finished part? Once that is clear, the team can choose relevant evidence and see what it can—and cannot—establish.

sections.title: Cooling produces gradients through the wall and across the part
sections.text: Heat leaves a moulding through its contact with the tool, while the interior cools through the part thickness. Geometry, local wall thickness, mould surface condition, circuit layout and local flow history mean that different regions need not experience the same thermal path. In a semi-crystalline grade, time and temperature also affect the opportunity for ordered regions to develop. In reinforced grades, flow can orient fibres differently from place to place. The final component can therefore contain local differences in structure and response even though it came from one shot of one grade. This is why a single average temperature or family description cannot fully explain a local dimensional result.

sections.title: Read shrinkage and warpage as part-level outcomes
sections.text: Shrinkage describes a dimensional change relative to a defined mould or test reference; warpage describes a shape change that can arise when different areas or directions respond unequally. They are related outcomes, but they are not synonyms and neither is explained by polymer family alone. Material structure, formulation, flow orientation, local pressure and thermal history can all contribute. A useful investigation compares dimensions at defined locations and directions, records the part's measurement condition, and checks whether the pattern repeats across cavities and cycles. Use current grade data and the real part's acceptance requirements; a generic shrinkage value or a standard test specimen cannot guarantee the dimensions of a different production geometry.

chapters.title: How melted plastic flows: viscosity and shear
chapters.applicability: A plain-language introduction to melt flow. Exact measurements apply only at stated material, temperature and flow conditions.

sections.title: Start here: why melted plastic does not flow like water
sections.text: Viscosity is a word for how strongly a fluid resists flowing. Honey has more flow resistance than water, which is a helpful first comparison. Melted plastic is more complicated: its flow resistance can change with temperature and with how quickly it is being pushed. The rate at which nearby layers slide past each other is called shear rate. Many plastic melts become easier to move when pushed faster; this is called shear-thinning. The machine’s pressure reading reflects resistance across a route that may include the nozzle, channels and cavity. It is not automatically a direct measurement of pressure everywhere inside the part.

sections.title: Viscosity is a process response, not a fixed material number
sections.text: The apparent resistance of a polymer melt to flow depends on temperature, deformation rate and material state. Many thermoplastic melts exhibit shear-thinning behaviour, so the apparent viscosity can decrease as shear rate increases. This is one reason that flow rate, geometry and temperature interact strongly during filling instead of acting as independent knobs.

sections.title: Geometry converts rheology into pressure demand
sections.text: A polymer that flows acceptably through one runner and gate can demand much more pressure through a thinner, longer or colder path. Pressure loss therefore cannot be interpreted without considering the flow path, rate and thermal condition together. Machine pressure is an upstream response to the whole system, not a direct measurement of the cavity at every location.

sections.title: Use rheology to form hypotheses, then test the actual system
sections.text: Rheological principles help predict how changes may influence filling, but they do not remove the need for controlled studies. A useful process investigation combines the expected mechanism with repeatable observations such as fill progression, pressure response, part mass or appropriate cavity measurements. If the observations disagree with the prediction, revise the model rather than forcing the data to fit it.

sections.title: Shear-thinning explains why flow rate changes pressure demand
sections.text: Many thermoplastic melts show shear-thinning behaviour: their apparent viscosity can fall as the rate of deformation increases. Injection flow is not uniform throughout the path, so different regions can experience different rates and temperatures at the same time. A viscosity number measured at one temperature and test rate is therefore not a complete description of what the melt will do in another gate or cavity. When filling behaviour changes, compare the exact grade and material condition, the rate actually achieved, the thermal state and the geometry. A family label or one flow index can help form a question, but cannot alone predict the pressure needed in a production mould.

sections.title: Follow pressure through the path and identify the sensor
sections.text: Melt passes through a sequence that may include the screw tip, nozzle, sprue, runner, gate and cavity. Each section contributes to the system response, and the narrowest visible feature is not automatically the only source of pressure loss. A machine pressure sensor describes pressure at its own location and can include losses downstream; it is not a direct cavity-pressure measurement. Cavity sensors, where installed, answer a different question and are also location-specific. Before comparing traces, name the sensor, timing and control phase, then relate the signal to achieved motion and the part result. This keeps pressure useful as evidence without treating it as a unique diagnosis.

chapters.title: Moisture and drying
chapters.applicability: General information about moisture-sensitive plastics. Drying conditions and allowed moisture levels are grade-specific; use current supplier instructions.

sections.title: Start here: why some plastics need drying
sections.text: Some plastics take moisture into the material, even when their surface looks dry. A surface that was splashed is different from moisture absorbed into the plastic. Drying is a controlled way to remove absorbed moisture before processing, but the required method and target depend on the exact grade. In a moisture-sensitive plastic, water can react with the material while it is hot; this reaction is called hydrolysis and can weaken the long polymer chains. A dryer’s screen tells you about the dryer’s settings or readings. It does not, by itself, prove how much moisture is in the plastic that reaches the machine.

sections.title: Moisture can affect appearance, processing and polymer integrity
sections.text: Moisture effects depend on polymer chemistry. It can contribute to surface defects, foaming and unstable plasticising, and in hydrolysis-sensitive polymers moisture present at melt temperature can reduce molecular weight. Drying is therefore a material-control task, not merely a cosmetic adjustment.

sections.title: There is no universal drying recipe
sections.text: Supplier documents demonstrate materially different drying requirements between polymer families and grades. A time-and-temperature pair copied from another resin can be ineffective or harmful. Confirm the exact material and grade, incoming or measured moisture condition, dryer capability and current supplier requirement before setting a drying process.

sections.title: Keep the material dry after drying
sections.text: Drying performance can be lost if dried hygroscopic material is exposed to humid air during conveying, storage or machine feeding. The material path from dryer to feed throat is part of the controlled process and should be assessed when moisture-related evidence persists.

sections.title: Separate moisture evidence from similar-looking symptoms
sections.text: Surface streaks, bubbles, degradation or unstable processing can be consistent with moisture, but appearance alone does not prove it. Compare material history, measured moisture where appropriate, dryer condition, timing, affected lots and the response to controlled handling. If the symptom persists with verified material condition, widen the diagnosis to other volatile, thermal, contamination, machine or mould mechanisms instead of repeatedly increasing drying severity.

sections.title: Follow conditioned material from the container to the feed throat
sections.text: A drying record describes only part of the material's journey. The grade and lot, container opening history, dryer status, conveying route, hopper exposure and point of sampling all affect whether a moisture result represents the pellets entering the machine. A measurement taken before a long or exposed transfer may not describe the material at the feed throat. When symptoms change between lots or after interruptions, compare the material-handling history as well as the dryer display. Use the supplier's current method and grade-specific limit; this chapter does not supply a universal target.

sections.title: Distinguish absorbed moisture from a wet material surface
sections.text: Some polymers take up moisture within the material, while moisture can also reach pellets through exposed storage, condensation or handling. The process consequence depends on the polymer chemistry and grade. In a hydrolysis-sensitive polymer, moisture present at melt temperature can damage the polymer; in other situations, water or another volatile may mainly affect appearance or plasticising stability. The symptom alone does not tell which condition is present. Identify the exact grade, review the current supplier limits and handling guidance, and use the specified measurement approach where applicable. This avoids applying a drying response to a problem that has another cause.

sections.title: A dryer display is not a material-condition measurement
sections.text: A controller may report air temperature or another dryer value, while the material entering the feed throat has a separate moisture condition. Loading, airflow, residence, exposure after drying, conveying route, leaks and sampling point can all affect how representative the record is. The relevant evidence is the actual grade requirement, the equipment record and a credible observation or measurement of the material at the appropriate point. Do not infer that pellets are within specification simply because the dryer is on or has reached a displayed setpoint. Exact dryer requirements and test methods come from the current grade-specific supplier guidance.

chapters.title: How heat and time affect plastic
chapters.applicability: General ideas about how heat and time can affect plastic. Supplier limits depend on the grade.

sections.title: Start here: the plastic remembers its heat and time
sections.text: Thermal history means the heat and time the plastic has experienced along its journey. Pellets may wait in a container, move through a heated barrel, pause in a nozzle or hot runner, and then enter the mould. Time spent hot in the equipment is often called residence time. Too much heat exposure or too much time can damage some materials; this is one form of degradation. A colour change or a mark can have several causes, so appearance alone is not proof. The exact limits depend on the supplier’s grade guidance and the actual machine and mould path.

sections.title: Treat degradation as an evidence problem
sections.text: Discolouration, odour, gas, deposits, viscosity change or mechanical-property loss can be consistent with degradation, but none alone proves it. Check actual melt conditions, residence pathways, interruptions, contamination and grade-specific limits before changing the process.

sections.title: Time and temperature act together
sections.text: A polymer's thermal history accumulates through drying where applicable, barrel residence, shear heating, hot-runner residence and interruptions. A temperature that is acceptable for a short period may become damaging when residence increases, and a nominally moderate setpoint does not prove the material has avoided excessive thermal exposure. Current grade-specific supplier limits and actual process history therefore matter more than a generic barrel-temperature number.

sections.title: Trace the material path, not only the barrel settings
sections.text: The melt experiences a path through the screw, barrel, nozzle and, where present, a heated runner before it reaches the cavity. Material throughput, shot size, recovery, interruptions and retained melt can change how long portions of material remain in heated regions. The displayed barrel setpoints describe controller targets at particular zones; they do not by themselves establish the actual temperature or residence history of every part of the melt. When comparing good and poor production periods, align the process timeline with material identity, pauses, restart events, recovery behaviour and the location of any observed defect. Then check the exact grade's current supplier limits.

sections.title: Use timing patterns to separate competing explanations
sections.text: A symptom that appears mainly after a stoppage, at start-up, or after a material change gives different evidence from a symptom present on every steady cycle. Discolouration, odour, deposits, black specks or a change in flow can be consistent with excessive thermal exposure, but contamination, material mix-up, moisture and equipment condition can produce overlapping signs. Record when the change begins and where it appears, then compare the process trace and material history that coincide with that change. A diagnosis becomes stronger when it explains the timing and predicts an observable response; one successful adjustment or purge is not, on its own, proof of cause.

chapters.title: Material families and exact grades
chapters.applicability: An orientation to broad polymer groups. A family name never identifies the exact grade or sets its production conditions.

sections.title: Start here: family name versus exact grade
sections.text:
A material family is a broad group name, such as polyamide or polycarbonate. Think of the family as a neighbourhood on a map: it helps you know which general area you are in, but it does not identify one particular house. The exact commercial grade is closer to a full street address. It identifies the product whose supplier information you need to read.

A grade name often contains a manufacturer’s name and a code. Extra letters or numbers may distinguish a reinforced, coloured, flame-retarded, impact-modified or otherwise changed formulation. The code is not a universal language: the same-looking letters can mean different things at different suppliers. Copy the complete designation from the approved material record or packaging, and check the current supplier document for that exact grade. If a suffix is missing, two materials that appear to share a family label may not be the same product.

Family names are still useful. They help you form questions about what evidence may matter, such as heat exposure, moisture, stiffness, toughness, appearance or dimensions. But a family label does not tell you the exact property values, a production window or whether the material suits a particular part. Those decisions depend on the identified grade and the relevant supplier and product requirements.

For a first comparison, write down three separate things: the broad family, the complete supplier grade and the requirement the part must meet. Keep them separate in your notes. If a document or conversation gives only a family name, mark the grade as unknown and resolve it before treating property data or processing advice as applicable.

sections.title: Families are useful maps, not recipes
sections.text: Polymer families help engineers anticipate broad differences in thermal behaviour, moisture sensitivity, stiffness, toughness, chemical resistance and processing demands. They are useful for asking better questions, but they do not define a production window.

sections.title: The grade is the actionable identity
sections.text: Two grades from the same polymer family may differ through molecular weight, reinforcement, flame retardants, impact modifiers, colour systems or processing aids. Production decisions should therefore resolve the full commercial grade and revision of its supplier information before relying on family-level guidance.

sections.title: Do not infer interchangeability from similar labels
sections.text: Two grades in the same polymer family may differ enough in reinforcement, viscosity, additive package or thermal stability that a process transferred between them behaves differently. When substituting material, treat the change as a new evidence question: confirm grade identity, supplier constraints, drying or conditioning requirements where applicable, and the product characteristics that must be reverified.

sections.title: Resolve the full material identity before comparing data
sections.text: Write down the manufacturer and complete grade designation, including formulation or colour suffixes that distinguish the supplied material. Then identify the current technical data and processing guidance for that exact grade, and note the conditions attached to any property value being compared. A family name, a similar abbreviation or a supplier's broad product page may point toward relevant information but cannot establish that two grades share a processing window. Keep substitution evidence tied to the actual material received and the part requirements that must be confirmed.

sections.title: Read a property table with its test conditions attached
sections.text: A datasheet value is evidence about a named grade tested under stated conditions. For each value, check the method, specimen dimensions, direction, conditioning, temperature, rate and units where supplied. A tensile or impact result from a standard specimen is useful for screening and comparison when the test bases match; it is not a direct promise of the response of a complex moulded part. A part may have different wall thickness, flow orientation, weld-line location and thermal history from the test specimen. Keep the test basis beside the number in any comparison so a difference in method or condition is not misread as a difference between materials.

sections.title: Start material selection from the part requirement
sections.text: First state what the component must do and where the evidence comes from: dimensional fit, impact response, stiffness, temperature exposure, chemical contact, appearance, electrical behaviour or another defined requirement. Then identify which grade-level data relate to that requirement and under what test conditions. Next check whether the supplier's processing guidance and the actual machine/mould system support a credible trial. Finally identify what must be measured on the production-like part to verify the choice. This sequence avoids selecting on one attractive datasheet number while overlooking a critical use condition, tool limitation, surface requirement or material-handling constraint.

sections.title: Worked example: compare the evidence before comparing the materials
sections.text:
Imagine a team is considering two hypothetical plastics for a moulded cover. The cover must fit with another component and remain intact in its intended use. No measured values are supplied in this example; it is a way to practise reading material information, not a recommendation for either candidate.

First, describe the part’s needs in plain language. “It must fit” is a start, but the team should identify which dimensions and use conditions define that fit. It should also say what “remain intact” means for this product. The part drawing, product requirements and site approval process control those definitions; a material datasheet cannot create them.

Next, write down the manufacturer and the complete grade designation for each candidate. If both are labelled with the same broad family name, do not assume they are equivalent. Check whether either grade has a formulation, colour or reinforcement suffix and whether the document is current. If the exact identity is missing, stop the comparison at that point and ask for the controlled material record or supplier information.

Then find the property evidence that relates to the requirement. Read the test method, specimen, conditioning, temperature, direction, units and any other conditions shown beside each value. Suppose one supplier reports a value from a dry specimen and the other reports a conditioned specimen, or the methods are different. Those entries may still be useful, but they are not a fair direct comparison until the difference is understood. Do not pick the larger number and call that material “better.”

Finally, record what the supplier data can answer and what it cannot. A standard-specimen value can help screen candidates. It does not by itself prove how the finished cover will fit after moulding or during use. The part geometry, moulding history and product verification still matter. A good beginner comparison therefore ends with a short list: exact grades confirmed, relevant evidence found, conditions compared, unknowns written down, and the required part-level checks identified.

sections.title: Review a substitution as a new evidence question
sections.text: A material substitution is not established by matching only the family abbreviation or a single published property. Confirm the exact old and new grades, formulation suffixes, colour, revision and supplier guidance. Compare the properties that matter to the product on a like-for-like test basis, then identify which process observations and part characteristics could change. Decide in advance what evidence would support the substitution and what result would require further review. A controlled comparison may show that the new grade behaves acceptably in the intended system, but that result applies to the tested material, tool, machine, part and conditions. It does not create a transferable recipe for other grades or moulds.

sections.title: Track regrind and recycled-feedstock history
sections.text:
A resin family and grade do not fully describe the feed after it has been recovered or processed again. For each comparison, record the exact grade and lot, where the returned material came from, whether it is plant-generated sprues or runners, rejected mouldings, or purchased recycled feedstock, and what blending or processing history is documented. Keep virgin resin, known in-house regrind, and post-consumer recycled material as distinct feed descriptions; they can have different histories and different kinds of uncertainty.

A regrind percentage describes a particular blend under a particular material and product specification. It is not a universal safe allowance or a transferable machine setting. The usable blend depends on the exact resin, feedstock source and preparation, supplier guidance, part requirements, customer or regulatory requirements, and the evidence from the intended process and product. Do not carry a percentage from one grade, part or supplier into another without review.

Research illustrates why the history matters, but does not supply a general limit. A 2021 study followed one polypropylene material through repeated plasticising, injection moulding, crushing and reprocessing, then measured fluidity and tensile properties. A 2025 study compared six post-consumer HDPE batches from one German municipal waste stream and related batch differences in composition and rheology to measured processing and product responses. The results apply to those materials and study conditions; they do not establish a maximum regrind fraction or predict another recycled feed.

For a material trial, identify the feed stream and lot before interpreting results. Agree which product-critical properties and dimensions must be checked, keep the blend and process records linked to sampled parts, and compare the results against the product’s controlled requirements. If the feed identity or history is uncertain, record that as an unresolved evidence question rather than treating a family name or blend percentage as proof of equivalence.

propertyGuide.title: Quick guide to common material properties
propertyGuide.intro: This guide covers the main measured property families used to understand and compare injection-moulding plastics; it is broad, not every specialist polymer test. Compare the exact grade, method, specimen, conditioning, direction, temperature, rate or load, and units. A datasheet value alone does not certify a moulded part.

rows.meaning: MFR reports the mass, and MVR the volume, of thermoplastic melt passing through a standard die during a timed test.
rows.readAs: Compare only with the same procedure, temperature, load and units. This is a test index, not a direct melt-viscosity measurement in the mould or a fill prediction.

rows.meaning: Capillary or slit-die tests show how melt flow resistance changes across defined shear conditions; this is a fuller flow curve than a single MFR/MVR index.
rows.readAs: Keep melt temperature, shear rate, die geometry and conditioning with the curve. It helps compare melt behaviour but does not predict a specific cavity fill by itself.

rows.meaning: A specimen is pulled in tension. Strength, modulus and elongation describe different aspects of its response; modulus is stiffness in that test.
rows.readAs: Keep specimen, direction, conditioning, temperature and test rate beside the values. A standard specimen does not by itself establish a finished part’s performance.

rows.meaning: A specimen is bent to measure flexural response; flexural modulus describes stiffness in that bending test.
rows.readAs: Do not swap flexural values for tensile values without checking the product question. Compare specimen dimensions, support span, method and conditioning.

rows.meaning: A specimen is squeezed to measure its compressive stress-strain response.
rows.readAs: Use the test direction, specimen shape, conditioning, temperature and rate. Compression results answer a different loading question from tensile or flexural values.

rows.meaning: A rapid impact test records how a defined plastic specimen responds to a blow.
rows.readAs: Notch, specimen configuration, conditioning and temperature affect the result. It is not a universal toughness score or a complete prediction of part impact performance.

rows.meaning: A durometer measures resistance to indentation using a stated Shore scale, such as A or D.
rows.readAs: Scale, specimen thickness, surface, dwell time and temperature matter. A Shore number is not a direct conversion to tensile strength or wear life.

rows.meaning: Dynamic mechanical tests measure a material's elastic and energy-losing response as temperature or test frequency changes.
rows.readAs: Storage modulus, loss modulus and tan delta are tied to test mode, frequency, temperature and specimen. They do not give one universal stiffness value for every part condition.

rows.meaning: Creep measures how a plastic specimen continues to deform over time while a load is held; tensile and flexural tests examine different loading modes.
rows.readAs: Compare only at similar stress, temperature, humidity, time and specimen conditions. Short-term strength cannot be substituted for long-term deformation.

rows.meaning: Fatigue testing studies damage or failure under repeated loading cycles; the cited method is for fibre-reinforced plastic composites.
rows.readAs: Stress ratio, direction, frequency, temperature, specimen and failure definition matter. A fatigue result for one reinforcement and loading setup is not a life guarantee for another grade or part.

rows.meaning: Differential scanning calorimetry measures heat-flow changes used to identify glass-transition behaviour, melting and crystallisation temperatures and enthalpies, and specific heat capacity.
rows.readAs: Sample history, heating or cooling rate, scan cycle, atmosphere and method affect interpretation. These events are not a mould temperature map or a single safe processing or service limit.

rows.meaning: The test reports the temperature at which a specimen reaches a specified deflection under a specified flexural load.
rows.readAs: Record the stress and method. HDT is a test result, not a guaranteed continuous-use temperature for a component.

rows.meaning: Vicat reports the temperature at which a loaded needle reaches a specified penetration in a thermoplastic specimen during heating.
rows.readAs: The chosen force and heating rate define the result. Vicat and HDT are different tests and neither by itself guarantees a continuous-use temperature.

rows.meaning: The coefficient describes how specimen length changes with temperature over a stated range.
rows.readAs: Direction, temperature range, test load and reinforcement orientation matter. Expansion measured on a standard specimen may not match every location in an anisotropic moulded part.

rows.meaning: These measurements describe how readily heat moves through a material and how quickly temperature changes spread through it.
rows.readAs: Method, temperature, specimen direction, fillers and fibre orientation matter. Material values alone do not determine mould cooling time, which also depends on part geometry, tool and contact conditions.

rows.meaning: Thermogravimetry tracks specimen mass as temperature or time changes under a stated atmosphere; it can reveal mass-loss steps and residual ash.
rows.readAs: Atmosphere, heating rate and sample preparation change the trace. A decomposition onset is not a recommended barrel setpoint or guaranteed processing limit.

rows.meaning: A standard injection-moulded specimen is measured to determine shrinkage under the method’s moulding and measurement conditions.
rows.readAs: Direction, elapsed time and conditioning matter. Test-specimen shrinkage does not guarantee a production part’s dimensions.

rows.meaning: Density is mass per unit volume of a non-cellular plastic specimen, determined by a stated method.
rows.readAs: Useful for comparing mass or composition evidence, but density alone does not describe stiffness, strength or impact behaviour.

rows.meaning: Water absorption measures uptake by a solid specimen during controlled exposure; water-content methods measure water in forms such as plastic granules.
rows.readAs: These are different measurements of different sample states. Neither result alone supplies a grade-specific drying setpoint.

rows.meaning: Immersion tests expose an unstressed plastic specimen to a specified liquid and measure changes after exposure.
rows.readAs: Chemical identity, concentration, temperature, duration, stress state and measured property matter. A result for one liquid and specimen does not establish universal compatibility.

rows.meaning: This test examines cracking of a thermoplastic held under strain while exposed to a chemical agent.
rows.readAs: Chemical agent, imposed strain, time, temperature and specimen preparation define the result. It is distinct from immersion testing of an unstressed specimen.

rows.meaning: Electrical tests may measure volume or surface resistivity, dielectric strength, or resistivity of conductive plastics.
rows.readAs: Separate conductive grades from insulating grades and keep voltage, frequency, electrodes, thickness, humidity and conditioning with results. These are different electrical behaviours, not one generic electrical rating.

rows.meaning: Fire tests measure specific behaviours such as ignition, burning progression or heat release under a defined apparatus and exposure.
rows.readAs: Test selection must match the product question. Specimen thickness, orientation, additives and conditioning affect results; a material test does not establish a product's regulatory approval or real-fire performance.

rows.meaning: Laboratory xenon-arc and fluorescent-UV exposures reproduce selected light, heat and moisture stresses to compare changes in plastics.
rows.readAs: Lamp spectrum, exposure cycle, moisture, temperature and endpoint matter. Accelerated exposure does not convert directly into a guaranteed number of outdoor service years.

rows.meaning: Optical tests measure visible light passing through transparent plastics and the scattering that makes a specimen look hazy.
rows.readAs: Thickness, surface, colour, crystallinity and specimen preparation affect the result. These tests do not replace colour or appearance specifications for a finished component.

rows.meaning: Size-exclusion chromatography estimates molecular-weight averages and the distribution of chain sizes in a polymer sample.
rows.readAs: Solvent, calibration, detector and sample preparation affect reported values. These advanced data are not normally a substitute for grade identity or measured melt-flow behaviour.

rows.meaning: Ash testing measures residue after a specified burn-off procedure and can help assess inorganic content in a plastic.
rows.readAs: The residue depends on resin chemistry, fillers, flame retardants and the selected procedure. Ash does not identify the filler or show fibre orientation in the moulded part.

rows.property: Friction and wear in polymer bearings (application-specific)
rows.meaning: Tribological tests measure friction and wear for defined polymer-bearing material pairs under specified sliding and lubrication conditions.
rows.readAs: The material pairing, load, speed, temperature, surface and lubrication define the result. Do not transfer bearing test values to unrelated moulded components.

comparisonExample.title: Worked comparison: two fictional polypropylene datasheets
comparisonExample.intro: Every value and grade name below is invented for teaching. The grades are not real products.

rows.interpretation: With the same stated method and conditions, grade B reports the higher MFR in this test. That does not prove it will fill a particular mould faster or reveal its full viscosity curve.

rows.methodAndConditions: ISO 527-1:2019 and ISO 527-2:2025; same specimen geometry, flow direction, conditioning, temperature and test speed
rows.interpretation: Grade B reports the higher tensile modulus in this matched test, meaning greater stiffness in that test. It does not mean higher tensile strength, impact toughness or better finished-part performance.

comparisonExample.takeaway: First check the full grade designation, test method, specimen, direction, conditioning, temperature, load or speed, and units. Compare only like-for-like results. Then choose what to investigate from the part's actual load, impact, temperature, moisture and chemical requirements; validate the selected grade in the moulded part.
comparisonExample.boundary: These synthetic numbers demonstrate comparison logic only. They are not supplier data, a grade recommendation, a processing instruction or proof of part performance.

chapters.title: Fibres, fillers and additives
chapters.applicability: General ways that fibres and additives can change a plastic. Effects depend on the exact formulation and processing history.

sections.title: Start here: what added ingredients can change
sections.text: A supplier may blend extra ingredients into the basic plastic. Glass fibres or mineral particles can make it stiffer; colourants, flame retardants or impact modifiers can change other properties. These ingredients are often called fillers, fibres or additives. They can affect several things at once, including how the plastic flows and how the finished part shrinks. In fibre-filled plastic, fibres can line up with the flow, like short pieces carried along by moving material. The part can then behave differently along the flow direction and across it. This difference between directions is called anisotropy. The exact effect depends on the complete grade and the part shape.

sections.title: Do not transfer settings between modified grades by name alone
sections.text: A reinforced, flame-retarded or otherwise modified grade should be treated as its own processing material. Confirm the supplier's grade-specific processing guidance and qualification requirements instead of assuming that settings for an unfilled or differently modified resin are interchangeable.

sections.title: Reinforcement can make response direction-dependent
sections.text: Short fibres tend to follow local melt flow, and the flow pattern can vary between the gate region, thin sections, turns, weld lines and the part surface. A reinforced moulding may therefore respond differently along the dominant flow direction and across it. The amount and direction of that difference depend on the exact formulation, geometry and moulding history. This is why a glass-filled grade cannot be treated as simply the unfilled grade with a higher stiffness value. Compare dimensions and mechanical requirements in the relevant directions and locations, and consult grade-specific data before interpreting a change in warpage or strength.

sections.title: Modifiers create coupled trade-offs
sections.text: Glass fibre, mineral filler, impact modifier, flame retardant, lubricant and colour system can each alter more than one aspect of the material. A formulation change may affect flow, shrinkage, directional behaviour, appearance, wear or thermal response together. The direction and size of those effects are grade-specific, so the modifier name alone is not enough to predict a production outcome. Resolve the exact commercial grade and its current documentation, then compare the part characteristics relevant to the application. If the supplier changes a formulation or a colour system, treat that as a material identity question and verify whether the change matters to the product and process evidence.

sections.title: Worked comparison: unfilled and reinforced candidates
sections.text: Imagine two candidate grades share the same base polymer, but one is unfilled and the other is glass-reinforced. The useful comparison begins with the part requirement, not the assumption that the reinforced option is automatically better. Identify which directions carry load, which dimensions control fit, where visible surfaces matter and whether the part has thin sections or divided flow. Match the supplier property tests and processing guidance to those questions. Then define what a production-like comparison must record: exact grade and lot, relevant process traces, cavity identity, part dimensions by location/direction, surface condition and the required mechanical check. The result can support a decision for that tested system; it cannot be copied as a universal setting or guarantee for another geometry.

chapters.title: How the machine melts and prepares plastic
chapters.applicability: A map of a common screw-based injection unit. Screw and valve designs, materials and operating limits vary by machine and plastic.

sections.title: Start here: turning pellets into a measured shot
sections.text: In a common machine, pellets fall from a hopper into a heated barrel. A rotating screw carries them forward, mixes them and helps soften them. This preparation step is called plasticising. As the screw turns, it also moves backwards to make room for the amount needed for a part. That measured amount of melt is called the shot. The screw's backward movement while it prepares the next shot is often called screw recovery. When the machine pushes the screw forward, a non-return valve helps keep the melt from flowing back. At the end of the push, the remaining forward screw position is called the cushion; display conventions vary by machine. These signals describe machine behaviour, but they do not alone prove that every part is identical.

sections.title: Plasticising must deliver both quantity and condition
sections.text: The screw and barrel do more than meter a volume of material. Rotation, heater input, back pressure where used, residence distribution and the non-return valve all influence how consistently the shot is prepared and delivered. A repeatable screw recovery time or position can be useful evidence, but neither alone proves uniform melt temperature, mixing quality or absence of degradation.

sections.title: The non-return valve is part of injection repeatability
sections.text: During injection the machine relies on the screw assembly to transfer force to the melt with limited backward leakage. Wear, contamination or inconsistent check-valve behaviour can alter delivered volume and pressure response. When cushion, part mass or transfer behaviour becomes unstable, the valve is one possible mechanism among several and should be evaluated using machine-specific procedures and repeatable evidence.

sections.title: Residence history links plasticising to material risk
sections.text: Material can experience different time-at-temperature histories depending on shot utilisation, recovery pattern, interruptions and the volume of melt retained in the system. For heat- or moisture-sensitive grades, the correct limits must come from current supplier and equipment documentation. Generic advice to increase temperature, back pressure or residence time should never replace grade-specific evidence.

sections.title: Separate preparation problems from injection-delivery problems
sections.text: An inconsistent shot can originate while the material is being prepared, while the shot is being transferred forward, or elsewhere in the flow path. Compare recovery behaviour, cushion or screw-end position, part mass, pressure response and timing to locate the likely stage. This avoids treating every weight or fill variation as evidence of one favourite component such as the check valve.

sections.title: A steady recovery trace does not prove an identical melt
sections.text: Recovery time and final screw position describe useful parts of shot preparation, but they do not directly measure temperature uniformity, mixing or material condition. Compare them with feeding behaviour, the injection response, cushion trend, part mass and any relevant quality change. If recovery stays steady while delivered shot or part response changes, look for causes downstream or in the machine's delivery system as well as in plasticising. If the recovery pattern changes first, investigate the preparation stage using the machine and material documentation. The aim is to locate where evidence first diverges, not to infer a component fault from one signal.

sections.title: Treat cushion as a repeatable signal with a defined reference
sections.text: Cushion is a screw-position observation at a particular point in the cycle, interpreted through that machine's position convention and control. A stable cushion trend can support the view that the measured end position is repeating, but it does not directly prove that the same melt mass entered every cavity. Part weight, recovery, transfer, the non-return function, sensor resolution and cavity balance can all affect the interpretation. Record where and when the signal is sampled, compare it across repeated cycles and relate it to cavity-specific part results. If cushion varies, investigate the whole shot-preparation and delivery path rather than declaring a worn valve from one signal alone.

chapters.title: Shot size and machine capacity
chapters.applicability: Concepts for a screw-based machine. Machine capacity and supplier limits must be checked for the actual process.

sections.title: Start here: how much plastic the machine prepares
sections.text: A shot is the measured amount of melt used for one injection. It must cover the part and the mould's feed channels, where those channels are part of the shot. Screw position records where the screw is during preparation and injection. Cushion is the remaining screw position after the injection sequence; it can help show whether the shot is repeating consistently. Shot utilisation means how the shot size compares with the machine's capacity. Machine suitability is more than whether the shot seems big or small. The machine must also handle the material, prepare it consistently and meet the needs of the mould and part. There is no one percentage that proves a machine is suitable for every job.

sections.title: Avoid universal shot-utilisation percentages
sections.text: A machine can be too large or too small for a process for several reasons, including residence exposure, plasticising capacity, available injection pressure or rate, metering repeatability and clamp requirements. A single universal percentage cannot establish suitability. Evaluate the machine, material, mould and required process window together.

sections.title: Nominal machine capacity is not the same as a suitable shot
sections.text: A machine's published maximum shot capacity is a rating under a defined basis; the process uses a particular material, shot size, screw configuration, cycle and hot-runner arrangement. Suitability depends on whether the machine can prepare and deliver the required shot repeatably within the relevant residence, recovery, pressure, rate and clamp constraints. A shot that occupies a very different portion of the available capacity can change how long material remains in the plasticising unit, but no single utilisation percentage is a universal acceptance rule. Confirm the rating basis and machine guidance, then assess the actual production configuration and measured response.

sections.title: Use several signals to understand shot consistency
sections.text: Shot consistency is an inference from repeated evidence, not a property of one number. Compare screw position and cushion using the machine's reference convention, recovery time, achieved injection response, part mass and cavity-to-cavity variation. Keep the material grade and lot, mould condition and sampling method comparable. If one signal is stable while the parts vary, the signal may simply be blind to the source of variation. If several signals move together, the pattern can narrow the investigation but still needs to be checked against the physical process and product measurements.

chapters.title: How the machine controls filling speed and pressure
chapters.applicability: General filling-control concepts. Controller names, measurements and limits vary by machine.

sections.title: Start here: the machine’s request and its response
sections.text: During filling, the machine asks the screw to move forward at a chosen speed. That request is the commanded speed. The measured screw movement is the achieved speed, and it may be lower if the machine reaches a pressure limit. Pressure describes how concentrated a push is over an area. In physics, pressure is force divided by area. The same force over a smaller area creates more pressure, like pressing with one fingertip instead of a flat palm. Pressure and force are related, but they are not the same thing. A machine pressure reading comes from a particular measuring location and does not automatically show the pressure inside the cavity. A transfer is the point where the machine changes from filling to the next part of the cycle, often holding pressure. The exact controls and signal names vary by machine. To understand a cycle, compare what was requested with what actually happened and check where each pressure measurement comes from.

sections.title: Rate changes can alter several physical conditions at once
sections.text: Changing filling rate can change pressure demand, shear history, thermal loss, flow-front timing and the way gas is displaced. A part response that improves after a rate change therefore does not identify which mechanism caused the improvement. Use the change as evidence and test the competing explanations rather than turning the successful setting into a universal rule.

sections.title: Separate a pressure limit from a velocity setting
sections.text: During velocity-controlled filling, the controller requests a screw-motion rate while the pressure limit constrains how much force the machine can apply. If the melt and flow path require more pressure than that limit permits, achieved motion can fall below the requested rate. Increasing the velocity command alone may then produce little change in actual filling. Read the velocity command, achieved response and pressure trace together, and check where each signal is measured. The trace can suggest whether filling is pressure-limited, but part or cavity evidence is still needed to judge the moulding outcome.

sections.title: Commanded filling velocity and achieved motion can differ
sections.text: During velocity-controlled filling, the machine attempts to follow a motion command while pressure develops to overcome resistance through the system. The command, achieved screw motion and measured pressure describe different parts of that response. If the machine reaches a configured pressure limit, the achieved motion can fall below the requested motion. A trace that shows this interaction should be read with the material condition, flow path, sensor location and part outcome; it is not proof that the pressure limit or one process setting is the root cause. The exact control display and limit behaviour depend on the machine.

sections.title: Transfer marks a change in control objective
sections.text: Fill-to-pack transfer changes what the control system is trying to govern as the cavity moves from filling toward post-fill pressure. Position, time, pressure or cavity-related criteria may be available depending on the machine and instrumentation, but their meaning depends on the actual moulding system. A copied transfer percentage is not evidence that the cavity is filled at the same point in another mould or grade. Compare the transfer signal with filling motion, pressure response and the resulting part across repeatable cycles. Use the machine's control definitions and the product/process limits that govern the application.
